Package hu.bme.mit.theta.frontend.transformation.model.types.complex.compound

Class ObjectLayout

java.lang.Object
hu.bme.mit.theta.frontend.transformation.model.types.complex.compound.ObjectLayout
public final class ObjectLayout extends Object
The byte-exact layout of a C object: where each member starts, and how much room the whole thing takes. This is the AD7 foundation -- the model in which a union member and its sibling name the same bits, and a `char[16]` view of a struct sees that struct's bytes.

It is deliberately pure: a function from a CComplexType and an architecture to offsets. It computes layout; it does not decide how a program addresses it. Nothing in the frontend calls it yet -- wiring it into member access is the separate, riskier half of AD7, and keeping the arithmetic independently testable is what makes that half checkable.

Everything is in bits, because bitfields have no byte-granular position. Sizes and alignments of whole objects are still byte multiples, as C requires.

What it implements

The System V rules every target in the benchmark set follows: a member starts at the next offset that satisfies its alignment, a struct's alignment is its strictest member's, a struct's size is rounded up to that alignment (so arrays of it stay aligned), and a union's members all start at zero. Bitfields pack into storage units of their declared base type and a zero-width bitfield closes the current unit.

Layout attributes

__attribute__((packed)) and ((aligned(n))) change layout, and both are honored: packed drops every member to byte alignment and removes tail padding, aligned(n) raises an object's or a member's alignment. A member's own aligned(n) wins over its struct's packed, which is what GCC does. They reach here through CStruct, which the TypeVisitor now populates from the attribute lists the grammar was already parsing (and previously discarded).

Unnamed bitfields

An unnamed bitfield (int : 3;, int : 0;) holds no value, so it gets no field -- nothing can name it, and giving it a storage cell would shift every following member in the wired cell model. It does move where the next member sits, though, so CStruct.Padding records it separately and the walk below replays it in declaration order. int : 0; closes the current storage unit, which is the whole reason the idiom exists.

    • alignBits

      public static int alignBits(CComplexType type, ArchitectureConfig.ArchitectureType arch, ObjectLayout.Attributes attributes)
      The alignment [type] demands, in bits.

      A scalar aligns to its own size, capped by the architecture's widest scalar alignment: the i386 quirk that an 8-byte long long or double aligns to 4 is exactly this cap. Types at least 128 bits wide (long double, __int128) align to their size on LP64 instead, which is what the x86-64 psABI specifies. An _Atomic scalar bypasses the cap entirely and always aligns to its own size.
